https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-brics-stra.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MRpX Modi will be hosting the leaders of Russia and China for a two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi (file photo) Image: Suo Takekuma/REUTERS Advertisement India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019. The summit comes at an important moment for India . As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia , and its relationship with Washington remains difficult . Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit. India's difficult BRICS chairship To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains. New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order. Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy. "These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW. However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal . India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powers Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier. International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access. The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment. Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset. "The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha. "It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations. BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11. With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine . The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran . Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis , forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead. With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage. "Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation. "BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added. Fears of Chinese dominance The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China. Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West. India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency. What is BRICS Pay? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'" "Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements." India's 'America Plus' strategy Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China. EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW. "India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University. But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns. "A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said. In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West. The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform. https://hvg.hu/itthon/20261111_pinter-be.text: Hajtó Péter a 2024-es választáson a Borkai Zsolttal Közösen a Jövőnkért Egyesület színeiben jutott mandátumhoz. Jelentős vagyoni hátrányt okozó hűtlen kezelés bűntettének gyanúja miatt nyomozást rendelt el a Veszprém Megyei Rendőr-főkapitányság a Borkai Zsolttal Közösen a Jövőnkért Egyesület színeiben képviselői mandátumot szerző Hajtó Péter, a Borkai-kampány volt kampányfőnöke és annak élettársa által az Ipari Park Kft.-nél összesen bruttó 30,7 millió forint közpénzért készíttetett, mesterséges intelligenciával generált tanulmányok ügyében – közölte Pintér Bence, Győr polgármestere a Facebook-oldalán. „A dokumentum a borítóval együtt 37 oldal, hol magyar, hol angol nyelvű, minden oldalán a mesterséges intelligenciával generált tartalmakra jellemző általános, semmitmondó, haszontalan sallangok, angol kulcsszavak, hasraütésszerű számok, Győrt sikertelenül ábrázolni próbáló képek vannak” – tette hozzá. Pintér Bence állítása szerint még augusztusban tett feljelentést ismeretlen tettes ellen, és bejegyzésében megosztott egy dokumentumot, arról, hogy a Legfőbb Ügyészség a nyomozás feletti ügyészi felügyeletet Győrből Veszprémbe helyezi át a pártatlan eljárás biztosítása, az elfogult ügyintézés látszatának elkerülése miatt. Győr polgármestere bejegyzésében arról is írt, hogy augusztusban javasolta közgyűlésnek, hogy Hajtó Pétert fosszák meg a bizottsági tisztségeitől és tagságától, és ezzel a plusz díjazásától. „A közgyűlés leszavazta, vizsgálatot kértek az Ipari Park Kft anyacégétől, a Győr-Szoltól. A vizsgálat lezajlott, a leánycég ügyvezetője érdemben nem tudta igazolni, mi szükség volt ezekre a megrendelésekre” – jegyezte meg, és hozzáfűzte, a következő közgyűlésre a korábbi beterjesztés tárgya mellett azt is kérni fogja, hogy távolítsák el mind az Ipari Park Kft., mind a Győr-Pér Repülőtér Kft. éléről is. Hajtó Péterre büntetővégzésben pénzbüntetést szabtak ki kényszerítés miatt, azonban ő tárgyalást kért. A bíróság egy hónapra elrendelte Orbán Áron letartóztatását, ott voltunk, amikor ezt követően rendőrautóban vitték el a Fővárosi Törvényszékről.

https://balkaninsight.com/2026/11/02/pol.text: An attempt to replace the leadership of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal has brought a row over judicial independence to a head, pitting the government against the president and raising fresh questions about the limits of their powers. A decade-long dispute over who controls Poland’s highest court escalated over the weekend, when a group of judges sought to remove its leadership, police were deployed to the building, and President Karol Nawrocki cut short a foreign trip to intervene. The next flashpoint is seen on Tuesday, November 3, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – one of the five judges elected by the current parliamentary majority but prevented from taking up their duties by the country’s president – has called a general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges to approve the court’s proposed budget for 2027. With the existing leadership, led by the court’s president Bogdan Swieczkowski, continuing to dispute her authority, it remains unclear whether the meeting can proceed as planned. The battle over the makeup of the Constitutional Tribunal, which has the power to overturn laws that violate Poland’s constitution and should act as an independent check on government and parliament, dates back to 2015, when both the outgoing centrist government and its right-wing successor made contested appointments to it. During Law and Justice’s (PiS) subsequent eight years in power, major reforms to the judiciary raised concerns over political interference and brought Poland into prolonged conflict with European institutions over the state of the rule of law in the country. Reversing those reforms was among Donald Tusk’s central campaign promises before his coalition took office in 2023, and his pro-European government has made restoring the court’s independence an essential part of repairing the country’s democratic institutions. The Tusk-led government has since refused to recognise the Tribunal’s legitimacy in its current form, but attempts to change the system through legislation have been blocked by opposition-aligned presidents. The immediate deadlock concerns five judges elected by the current parliament whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. These judges subsequently took their oaths without him, but the Tribunal’s leadership prevented them from hearing cases. In October, the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s constitutional advisory body, concluded that the president could not use his role in the appointment process to obstruct duly elected judges from taking office. However, PiS and President Nawrocki accuse Tusk of using unlawful methods to replace the court’s leadership with judges sympathetic to his government. The competing claims came to a head on Friday, when the five judges attempted to assert their authority over the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska announced the suspension of its president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, and declared herself the court’s acting head. The existing leadership rejected the move, leaving the institution with rival claims to authority. Separately, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek sought to have Swieczkowski and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski, stripped of judicial immunity, potentially paving the way for criminal charges over their alleged obstruction of the Tribunal’s work. The announcement brought more protesters to the Tribunal’s grounds in Warsaw, where supporters of the opposition had already been demonstrating for weeks against attempts by the newly elected judges to take up their posts. Senior PiS politicians joined the crowd, while police increased their presence around the building. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki cut short a state visit to Senegal, ordering his plane to turn around over Spain and return to Warsaw. He arrived at the Tribunal in the early hours of Saturday, challenged the authority of the judges seeking to take control, and helped the court’s deputy president enter the building. “Last night, Poland’s constitutional order was violated, and a constitutional state institution was forcibly taken over,” Nawrocki said in a statement issued shortly after 05:00 on Saturday morning. He demanded that police withdraw from the premises and announced emergency consultations with parliamentary party leaders. In a televised address on Saturday evening, Prime Minister Tusk defended the intervention, accusing PiS and the PiS-aligned presidents Andrzej Duda and his successor Nawrocki of perpetuating the crisis. “Nobody had any doubt that the Tribunal, in the form imposed by PiS, was not a real court,” he said, arguing that repeated attempts to resolve the dispute through legislation had been blocked. Tusk compared the situation to a thief who steals an elderly woman’s handbag, then complains of violence when caught, while bystanders suggest dividing the stolen money between the thief and the victim. “On certain matters, there can be no compromise,” he said. A constitutional reset to end an undignified row? Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, a leading civil liberties organisation, questioned whether Friday’s intervention by the government would help restore the Tribunal’s authority, calling the escalation “extremely harmful”. “The confrontations between judges and the President of the Republic of Poland outside the entrance to the Tribunal building undermine the dignity and authority of state institutions,” the organisation said in a statement. The European Commission weighed in on Saturday, backing the Polish parliament’s authority to appoint Tribunal judges. Meanwhile, US Ambassador Tom Rose warned that crowds outside the court risked worsening an already volatile situation. “The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals out of control,” he wrote on X, while stressing that Washington did not intend to interfere in Poland’s domestic affairs. With parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027, Tusk’s coalition faces pressure to deliver on its promise to restore judicial independence, while the opposition has made resistance to the government’s intervention a central issue. In August, Tusk announced that he was determined to ensure the newly elected judges could take up their posts at the Tribunal by September, even if the process was not particularly elegant. Speaking at the Campus Polska Przyszlosci event, he said he needed to be certain that “our judges will enter that building”. On Saturday afternoon, Nawrocki held meetings with parliamentary party leaders to discuss possible solutions. Among the proposals put forward by parties as far apart as the left-wing Razem and the far-right Confederation was a constitutional reset of the Tribunal, involving the replacement of all its sitting judges with a new bench appointed through a cross-party agreement.
